subject: history
title: Decline of the Witch Craze 1690-1750
welcome_lead: How scepticism, science and law dismantled official witch-hunting.
meta_desc: -Level adventure on the decline of the witch craze: scepticism, Enlightenment science and the 1735 Witchcraft Act.
final_note: You can explain why prosecutions ceased even as popular belief persisted.

walkthroughs.body_html: Reginald Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) had argued early that confessions were coerced. Late 17th-century scepticism drew on the Royal Society's empirical methods, Cartesian dualism and Newtonian mechanics. Balthasar Bekker's De Betoverde Weereld (1691-93) attacked the diabolic worldview from within Calvinism. Christian Thomasius (1701) criticised torture and witch trials in the Holy Roman Empire.

English assize judges (e.g., Sir John Holt, Chief Justice 1689-1710) became reluctant to convict. The 1712 trial of Jane Wenham ended in a royal pardon. In Scotland, the last execution is traditionally Janet Horne at Dornoch in 1727. France's last execution was 1745. Lay belief lingered but prosecutorial elites no longer cooperated.

The Witchcraft Act 1735 repealed the 1542, 1563 and 1604 statutes and the Scottish Act of 1563. It made it a crime to claim magical powers (punishable by up to a year's imprisonment and the pillory). Witchcraft was reclassified as imposture. Popular witch-belief survived in cunning folk, mobs (Tring 1751) and folklore; but the state had withdrawn its sanction.

mcqs.q: Did the Battle of Bosworth in 1485 end the Wars of the Roses?
options: Bosworth in 1485 ended the Wars of the Roses immediately.
It killed Richard III and put Henry Tudor on the throne, but Yorkist threats (Simnel 1487, Warbeck 1490s) continued — the wars only truly ended with Stoke Field in 1487.
Bosworth was a naval battle fought off the south coast of England.
They were a religious war between Catholics and Protestants.
